passage: Dear Diary, today at lunch break everyone crowded around Yusuf's new spectacles. Somebody started calling him 'Owl Eyes' and then like eight of us were saying it and hooting. I hooted too. Loud. It felt like my voice was mixed up with everyone's, so it didn't really count, and nobody was even looking at me. But when Yusuf took off his glasses and wiped them on his shirt and didn't look up, my stomach went funny. If it was only me and him, I would never say that. I don't even think owls are funny. Tomorrow I will sit next to him at lunch and say sorry, even if the others laugh. — Reena

qa.q: What name did the group start calling Yusuf?
qa.a: Somebody started calling him 'Owl Eyes' because of his new spectacles.

qa.q: How did Reena feel when Yusuf wiped his glasses and didn't look up?
qa.a: Reena's stomach went funny: Reena felt guilty and could see the hooting had really hurt Yusuf 😔

qa.q: What choice does Reena make at the end of the entry?
qa.a: Reena decides to sit next to Yusuf at lunch and say sorry, even if the others laugh, owning the choice alone instead of hiding in the group.

qa.q: What is it like for Yusuf when eight classmates hoot at once?
qa.a: For Yusuf it is one wall of noise with nobody single to answer, so he hides behind wiping his glasses and not looking up.

grounding: Shows a child joining classmates' teasing because their own voice feels lost in the group, something they would not do one to one.

passage: Class Four spilled out of the school gate in Rampur like marbles from a tin. Near the handpump, Seema's milk can tipped, and white streaks ran into the dust. Someone shouted, "Doodh-gaadi crashed!" and in a blink ten children were chanting it, stamping in rhythm. Leela, who never even raised her hand in class, heard her own voice join in, then add a new line about Seema's torn chappal. It felt easy, like singing at the temple fair where nobody hears just you. Then Seema's grandmother came round the corner with a bucket. Her eyes found Leela, only Leela. "You too, beti?" Leela's face went hot. The chant fell apart. She picked up the empty can and handed it back without a word.

qa.q: What did the children chant after Seema's milk can tipped?
qa.a: Ten children chanted "Doodh-gaadi crashed!", stamping in rhythm.

qa.q: Why did Leela's face go hot when the grandmother spoke?
qa.a: Leela felt ashamed once she was seen alone, only Leela, and could no longer hide inside the chant.

qa.q: What turning point changes what Leela does next?
qa.a: When Seema's grandmother looks straight at Leela and asks "You too, beti?", Leela stops, picks up the empty can and hands it back.

qa.q: How might Seema see Leela joining the chant?
qa.a: Seema might feel extra hurt because Leela, usually so quiet, even added a line about the torn chappal, so it seemed as if everyone had turned at once.

grounding: Illustrates a quiet child swept into group teasing at a village handpump, feeling unseen until one adult picks them out.

passage: On the coach back from the zoo, the back row belonged to Felix's class. When Aiko, three rows ahead, laughed her high, hiccuping laugh, Jonas squeaked it back. Then five boys squeaked it, then eight. Felix pulled his hood up and squeaked loudest of all. Under the hood he was just part of the noise, one of many grey sweatshirts, and the coach rocked with laughter. At the rest stop, though, Felix ended up alone at the hand dryer beside Aiko. She was quiet, drying her hands for much longer than she needed to. He opened his mouth and realised he could not make that sound to her face, not in a million years. "Nice penguins today," he mumbled instead, and felt his ears burn.

qa.q: Where did Felix end up alone beside Aiko?
qa.a: At the rest stop, Felix ended up alone at the hand dryer beside Aiko.

qa.q: What do Felix's burning ears suggest he is feeling?
qa.a: Felix seems embarrassed and guilty, because alone with Aiko he knows he could never make that sound to her face.

qa.q: What could Felix choose to do now that the hood is off?
qa.a: Felix could say sorry to Aiko for the squeaking and refuse to join in on the ride home, even if the back row carries on.

qa.q: Why might Aiko have dried her hands for much longer than she needed to?
qa.a: Aiko may have been hurt and putting off going back to the coach, where so many voices had been copying her laugh.

grounding: Shows a boy hiding under a hood inside a squeaking back row, doing what he could never do to the girl's face.

passage: After Saturday swimming class at the sports club, the girls' changing room echoed like a well. Lakshmi, the newest, came out in a big frilly costume and orange armbands. Someone said, "Quack quack," and then six girls were quacking and flapping their elbows. Bidisha, ten, quacked too, loud, her voice lost among the others. It didn't feel like her; it felt like the room. Lakshmi pulled a towel round herself and sat on the bench. On Monday the coach paired Bidisha and Lakshmi for kicking practice, just the two of them at the shallow end. Bidisha couldn't look at her. Halfway through, she held out her spare goggles. "These don't leak," she mumbled.

qa.q: What was Lakshmi wearing when she came out?
qa.a: She came out in a big frilly costume and orange armbands.

qa.q: Why did quacking in the changing room not feel like Bidisha's own act?
qa.a: Her voice was lost among six others, so she felt the room was doing it, not her, and nobody would single her out.

qa.q: What turning point shows Bidisha she would never have teased Lakshmi alone?
qa.a: When the coach paired them at the shallow end, she could not even look at Lakshmi, so she offered her spare goggles instead.

qa.q: How might Lakshmi have felt sitting on the bench with the towel round her?
qa.a: As the newest girl, she probably felt humiliated and alone against a whole room, with nobody in particular to answer.

grounding: A ten-year-old joins a group's teasing in a changing room that she would never do alone, because her voice feels lost in the crowd.

passage: I'm Lavanya, Charu's older sister. This was our cousin's wedding. Little Mohit had come in his father's kurta, which reached his ankles. About twelve of us cousins crowded round him. Someone whispered, "Tent!" and then everyone was chanting it. Charu, nine, who usually hands sweets to the smallest children, chanted loudest, clapping. Mohit stood holding the hem of the kurta. Then the band stopped all at once, and in the silence one voice rang out: "TENT!" It was Charu's. A hundred heads turned. I watched her face go from pink to white. She ran to Mohit and straightened his kurta sleeve, as if that could undo it. I don't know what she felt, but she stayed by him all evening.

qa.q: Why did Mohit's kurta reach his ankles?
qa.a: He had come in his father's kurta.

qa.q: What does Charu's face going from pink to white suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she was shocked and ashamed once her voice was heard alone, because in the crowd the chant had not felt like hers.

qa.q: What did Charu do after the moment of silence, and was it a good choice?
qa.a: She went straight to Mohit and stayed by his side all evening, which was a kind way to show she was sorry, though saying sorry aloud would also help.

qa.q: What was the teasing like for Mohit?
qa.a: Mohit faced twelve children at once and could only stand holding the hem of the kurta, with no single person to stop.

grounding: A usually kind nine-year-old chants a cruel nickname with a crowd of cousins, and is shaken when her voice is heard alone.

passage: The substitute teacher had stepped out, and Class 6C at Hill View School grew loud in seconds. A group near the window started chanting "Chashmish! Chashmish!" at Hrithik, who had just got thick new glasses. Parul, eleven, never teased anyone; she was the girl who lent pencils. But everyone was laughing, the noise was huge, and nobody would notice one more voice. She joined in, quietly at first, then loudly. It felt oddly easy, as if the voice wasn't hers. Hrithik pushed his glasses up and stared at his desk, ears red. Then the door opened and the class teacher walked in. The chant died. She looked straight at Parul. "You too?" Parul's stomach dropped. Alone, under that look, she could hardly believe she'd done it. At recess the teacher sat with Hrithik, and Parul went over to say sorry.

qa.q: What were the group chanting at Hrithik?
qa.a: They were chanting "Chashmish! Chashmish!"

qa.q: Why did Parul join the chant?
qa.a: In the loud group Parul felt hidden and safe from being singled out, so it felt easy, as if the voice wasn't hers.

qa.q: What could Parul do if a class starts teasing someone again?
qa.a: Parul could stay quiet or say "stop" to the person next to her, remembering that each voice in a group is still someone's own choice.

qa.q: How might Hrithik have experienced the chant?
qa.a: Hrithik felt humiliated and alone, staring at his desk with red ears while the whole class seemed against him.

grounding: A child in a rowdy class joins teasing she would never do alone, feeling hidden by the group, until being singled out shows her what she did.

passage:
Monday: On the school bus, the back-seat group started flicking paper balls at Gargi, the new girl, and calling her "Miss Topper." Sonali, ten, watched, uneasy.
Wednesday: The back seat was louder. Everyone was doing it. Sonali, squashed in the middle, flicked one paper ball too. Nobody looked at her. It felt like the group did it, not her.
Friday: Gargi got off the bus crying. The bus aunty stopped Sonali at the step. "I saw you throw one." Sonali went hot all over. That evening she told her mother, who listened, then called Gargi's mother with her so Sonali could apologise herself. The next Monday, Sonali sat next to Gargi.

qa.q: What were the back-seat group calling Gargi?
qa.a: They were calling her "Miss Topper."

qa.q: What was Sonali feeling on Wednesday when she threw a paper ball?
qa.a: Sonali felt hidden in the group, as if the group did it rather than her, which made the teasing feel less like her choice.

qa.q: What did Sonali's mother do that helped, and why?
qa.a: She listened and helped Sonali apologise to Gargi that same evening, turning a hidden group act into a personal responsibility Sonali could repair.

qa.q: How might Gargi have felt on the bus that week?
qa.a: Gargi likely felt scared and humiliated, being new and targeted by a whole group, which is why she got off crying.

grounding: Over a week, a child in a rowdy bus group joins teasing she would never do alone, feeling nobody will single her out, until an adult names it.

passage: Bhavna, you think it's harmless because everyone was doing it? Let me tell you about the fair in Nashik when I was eleven. I'm Asif chacha, and there was a boy from our lane, a quiet one who stammered. At the Ganpati fair a whole gang of us followed him around, copying his words. I would never have done it alone; I liked him. But in the crowd, with the loudspeakers and the lights, it felt like nobody was me. I laughed loudest. Then an old man selling balloons stopped the gang, took the boy's hand, and asked each of us our names, one by one. When he asked mine, I couldn't speak. With my name in the air, I was just me again, and ashamed. He walked the boy home himself. The next day I went to the boy's house and said sorry to his face.

qa.q: What was the old man selling?
qa.a: He was selling balloons.

qa.q: What was Asif feeling when the old man asked his name?
qa.a: Asif felt ashamed and exposed, because being named made him responsible again instead of hidden in the crowd.

qa.q: Why was asking each child's name a turning point in the story?
qa.a: It broke the crowd's anonymity, so each boy had to face what he had done as himself.

qa.q: How might the boy who stammered have felt when the old man took his hand?
qa.a: The boy likely felt relieved and protected after being frightened and mocked by the whole gang.

grounding: An elder recalls joining a crowd that mocked a boy at a fair, feeling anonymous in the group, until being named made him face his own actions.

passage:
The school bus was stuck in traffic outside the zoo, and the fan above the back seats had stopped. Everyone was hot and cranky. The driver kept honking. Then someone at the back started a chant: "Squeaky, squeaky!" It was for Gurpreet, whose voice had begun to crack.
Jomon would never say that to Gurpreet's face. They sat together in maths. But twenty voices were chanting, and in the crowd of heads nobody could tell who was who. Jomon chanted too, laughing.
Gurpreet stared out of the window with red ears.
Ma'am turned round from the front seat. "Enough. Every one of you." She walked down the aisle and sat beside Gurpreet. Jomon stopped, his face burning.

qa.q: Where was the school bus stuck?
qa.a: It was stuck in traffic outside the zoo.

qa.q: Why did Jomon join the chant even though he sat with Gurpreet in maths?
qa.a: In a crowd of twenty voices he felt hidden and safe from blame, so he joined in something he would never do alone.

qa.q: What could Jomon do the next day?
qa.a: He could say sorry to Gurpreet on his own, without the crowd, and refuse to join the chant if it starts again.

qa.q: What is it like for Gurpreet when twenty voices chant at him?
qa.a: Gurpreet feels embarrassed and alone, staring out of the window with red ears while even a friend joins in.

grounding: Shows a child joining group teasing he would never do alone, because in a rowdy busload nobody seems to single him out.

passage:
Sabina was not a mean girl. Everyone said so. So nobody expected her to be part of it.
It began in the corridor after the bell. Five girls from her class started flicking paper balls at Ishita's new short haircut, laughing, "Boy cut! Boy cut!"
Sabina had her own paper ball in her hand before she knew why. It was easy. Nobody was looking at her. They were all one giggling crowd. She flicked it.
Ishita turned. Her eyes went straight to Sabina, the only one she had ever shared a tiffin with.
The ball dropped from Sabina's other hand. Suddenly she was not part of a crowd. She was just Sabina, and Ishita had seen her.

qa.q: What did the girls flick at Ishita?
qa.a: They flicked paper balls at Ishita's new short haircut.

qa.q: What did Sabina feel when Ishita's eyes went straight to her?
qa.a: She felt exposed and ashamed, as if the crowd had vanished and she was suddenly seen as herself.

qa.q: What small step could Sabina take now?
qa.a: She could go to Ishita, say sorry and tell the other girls to stop, instead of hiding back in the group.

qa.q: How might Ishita feel when she sees Sabina among the girls?
qa.a: Ishita is likely hurt and betrayed, because a friend she shared a tiffin with was part of the teasing.

grounding: Shows a kind child joining group teasing because in a giggling crowd nobody seems to be looking at her, until the target looks straight at her.

passage:
"Why were you shouting 'Mouse' with them in the canteen, Jeevan?"
"Ujjwal, everyone was shouting it."
"I heard your voice. I know your voice."
"It was just a joke. Twenty people were saying it."
"Would you say it if it was just you and me?"
"...No."
"Then why?"
"I don't know. It didn't feel like me. It felt like the whole table."
"It was you. It was still you."
"I'm sorry, Ujjwal. I really am."
"I sit alone at lunch now because of that name."
"Sit with me tomorrow. And if they start, I won't say it. I'll tell them to stop."

qa.q: What name was being shouted in the canteen?
qa.a: They were shouting "Mouse."

qa.q: What does Jeevan mean by saying it didn't feel like Jeevan?
qa.a: Jeevan felt lost in the group, as if the shouting belonged to the whole table, so Jeevan felt less responsible and less guilty in the moment.

qa.q: What could Jeevan do at lunch tomorrow?
qa.a: Jeevan could sit with Ujjwal and tell the others to stop if they start the name again.

qa.q: What is it like for Ujjwal because of the name?
qa.a: Ujjwal feels lonely and hurt, now sitting alone at lunch because of it.

grounding: Shows a child who joined canteen teasing because in the group it did not feel like their own act, then facing the classmate they hurt.

passage: Last Holi, a gang of us from Class 5 ran through the colony with water balloons. I'm Manoj, and on my own I'm quite quiet. But in that noisy crowd, all of us purple and green, it felt as if nobody could tell who was who. When we saw Uma hiding behind her gate because she hates colour, someone started chanting 'Scaredy Uma!' and I chanted too, louder than anyone. I even threw a balloon at the gate. Alone, I would never have done that. Uma is my neighbour; she lends me comics. She ran inside crying. Afterwards, washing off the colour, I felt sick. In the crowd it hadn't felt like me doing it. But it was. The next day I went and said sorry, and gave her my best comic.

qa.q: Why was Uma hiding behind her gate?
qa.a: Because she hates colour.

qa.q: How did Manoj feel washing off the colour afterwards?
qa.a: Manoj felt sick and ashamed, knowing he had joined in teasing he would never do alone.

qa.q: What could Manoj do next time a crowd starts chanting?
qa.a: He could remember that it's still him in the crowd, stay quiet or step out, and stand with the person being teased.

qa.q: How might Uma have felt hearing her neighbour chant with the crowd?
qa.a: Uma likely felt hurt and betrayed, since Manoj was a friend who borrowed her comics.

grounding: A boy looks back on joining a Holi crowd's teasing he would never do alone, feeling hidden in the group.

passage:
Class 6 note, winter picnic bus.
On the way back from the zoo, the back of the bus started chanting a rhyme about Vijay's thick glasses. It began with two boys and spread fast. I noticed Leela, who is usually gentle and had read quietly all the way there, singing loudest and banging the seat. When I walked down, it stopped. Leela went red and looked at the floor. She told me later, 'Everyone was doing it. It didn't feel like me.' Vijay sat with his face to the window. I sat next to him for the rest of the ride. At school I spoke to the back rows together, then to Leela alone; she asked to apologise to Vijay herself. I phoned Vijay's mother this evening and will check in with him tomorrow.

qa.q: What was the rhyme about?
qa.a: Vijay's thick glasses.

qa.q: How did Leela feel when the teacher walked down the aisle?
qa.a: Leela felt embarrassed and ashamed, going red and looking at the floor.

qa.q: What did the teacher's response get right?
qa.a: It stopped the chant, stayed with Vijay, spoke to the group and then to Leela privately, and let Leela make her own apology.

qa.q: What was the ride like for Vijay?
qa.a: Vijay felt hurt and humiliated, sitting with his face to the window while most of the bus sang about him.

grounding: A teacher's winter-trip note shows a gentle girl joining a bus crowd's teasing she would never do alone.

passage:
Diwali night.
Dear diary, I did something bad. On the terrace, all the colony kids were bursting crackers and being loud, and somebody started laughing at Keerthana's frock because it was last year's. Then everybody laughed, and somehow I was laughing too, and I even said 'hand-me-down queen'. It was dark and smoky and nobody could see who said what, and it felt like the noise said it, not me. Keerthana went downstairs. Then I saw her mother's face at the door. My stomach dropped. Keerthana helped me with fractions all summer! Amma asked why I was quiet, and I told her. She didn't shout. She said, 'Your name goes with you, even in the dark.' Tomorrow I'll go and say sorry, and take her some of our kaju katli.
Leela

qa.q: Why were the kids laughing at Keerthana's frock?
qa.a: Because it was last year's.

qa.q: What did Leela feel on seeing Keerthana's mother at the door?
qa.a: Leela felt a sinking guilt, stomach dropping, realising the teasing had hurt someone who had been kind.

qa.q: What does Amma's line 'Your name goes with you, even in the dark' teach?
qa.a: That being part of a noisy crowd doesn't remove responsibility; Leela still chose the words.

qa.q: How might Keerthana have felt going downstairs?
qa.a: Keerthana probably felt humiliated and hurt, mocked by a crowd that included someone she had helped.

grounding: A child's Diwali diary shows joining crowd teasing on a dark terrace and feeling it wasn't really them.

passage: The Christmas holidays were two days away, and the bus stop outside the panchayat school in Kuttanad was crowded and loud. Joseph arrived in an enormous brown sweater, sleeves folded three times. Someone shouted, "Appooppan sweater! Grandpa sweater!" Then five voices, then ten. Seema was in the middle of the knot of kids, and before she knew it her voice was in the chant too, loud and laughing. Nobody could tell which voice was hers. Joseph stared at the road. On the bus, Seema sat alone by the window. She would never have said it to Joseph by herself; last month he had shared his umbrella with her all the way home. Her stomach felt sour the whole ride.

qa.q: How many times were Joseph's sleeves folded?
qa.a: Three times.

qa.q: How did Seema feel on the bus afterwards?
qa.a: She felt guilty and uneasy, her stomach sour, because she had joined a chant she would never have said to Joseph alone.

qa.q: What could Seema do next?
qa.a: She could say sorry to Joseph, and next time step out of the chant or tell the others to stop instead of hiding in the crowd.

qa.q: What was it like for Joseph at the bus stop?
qa.a: It was likely humiliating and lonely to face ten laughing voices with no one to reason with, so he just stared at the road.

grounding: A child in a noisy group at a bus stop joins teasing she would never do alone, because in the crowd nobody can tell which voice is hers.
